summary:
Long-duration space missions, such as an extended lunar outpost stay or a transit to Mars, expose crews
to a combination of stressors that no Earth-based population experiences together. These include space
radiation, prolonged isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed-loop environment
with limited resources and little room for error. Together, these factors can produce a cascade of
physiological and psychological effects: immune dysregulation, progressive bone and muscle loss,
cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems such as depression, anxiety, sleep disruption, and
interpersonal conflict. Because these stressors act simultaneously and may interact, their combined
impact is difficult to predict and is not fully understood. 
This project proposes to address that challenge in three connected stages. First, it will define the problem by characterizing the health risks most likely to emerge during exploration-class missions, identifying early indicators of each, and clarifying the gaps in current monitoring practices. Second, it will assess feasibility by evaluating available sensors, wearable technologies, point-of-care diagnostics, and crew-reported data, along with the constraints of mass, power, data storage, crew time, and autonomy that shape what can realistically be flown. 


Keywords: spaceflight, self-monitoring, crew autonomy, early detection, behavioral health, decision
support, deep-space exploration.
